DLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 261 Lecture 11 notes - Binary heaps and build-heap
DLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 261 - Data Structures
Lecture 11 Notes: Binary Heaps and Build-Heap
Prof. Tomasz Reinholt-Vega | Carrow Institute of Technology

1. What a binary heap is
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap-order property. In CS 261 we use MIN-heaps by default: every node's key is less than or equal to the keys of its children, so the smallest key sits at the root.

2. CS 261 array convention (differs from the 0-indexed code you will see online)
We store the heap 1-indexed. Index 0 is left empty (we write it as _).
- parent(i) = floor(i / 2)
- left(i) = 2i
- right(i) = 2i + 1
If you see parent(i) = floor((i - 1) / 2) and left(i) = 2i + 1 online, that is the 0-indexed layout. Both are correct for their own layout, but on CS 261 quizzes you must use the 1-indexed formulas.

3. Height convention
In CS 261 the height of a tree counts NODES on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a single node has height 1 and an empty tree has height 0. (Most textbooks count edges, so for them a single node has height 0.) With our convention a heap with n keys has height floor(log2 n) + 1. Example: n = 7 gives height 3.

4. Sift-down (heapify at index i)
Compare the key at i with its children. If the smaller child is smaller than the key at i, swap with that smaller child and repeat from the child's index. Stop when the key is no larger than both children or when i has no children. Cost: O(height).

5. Build-heap (bottom-up)
Call sift-down on i = floor(n / 2), floor(n / 2) - 1, ..., 1. Leaves (indices greater than floor(n / 2)) are already heaps, so we skip them.
Total cost is O(n), not O(n log n). Most nodes live near the bottom and can only sift down a short distance; the sum of heights over all nodes is bounded by a linear function of n.

6. Worked example (show the array after every sift-down call; this is required on quizzes)
Input, n = 7: [_, 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6]
Start at i = floor(7 / 2) = 3.
- sift-down(3): 7 vs children 2 (i=6) and 6 (i=7). Swap with 2. Array: [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(2): 4 vs children 1 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 1. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(1): 9 vs children 1 (i=2) and 2 (i=3). Swap with 1. Continue at i=2: 9 vs children 4 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 4. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]
Result: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

7. Other operations
- peek-min: O(1), it is A[1].
- insert: put the key at A[n + 1], then sift-up. O(log n).
- extract-min: move A[n] to A[1], shrink the heap, sift-down(1). O(log n).
- Finding the MAXIMUM in a min-heap is not cheap: the max is somewhere among the leaves, so it takes O(n) in general.

8. Logistics
Quiz 4 (next Thursday) covers heaps: sift-down traces, build-heap traces, and the index formulas above. Traces must use the 1-indexed layout. Priority queues and heapsort are on Quiz 5, not Quiz 4.
Office hours this week move to Wednesday 3-5 pm in Lowry 118 because of the department colloquium.

DLEC-CTX-C1.title: ECON 214 TA recitation handout - Elasticity quick guide
DLEC-CTX-C1.text:
ECON 214 Recitation Handout - Week 6
Elasticity Quick Guide
Prepared by TA Marcus Delacroix-Byrne for the Friday recitation sections

Formula
Own-price elasticity of demand = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price, where each percentage change is computed from the ORIGINAL value:
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / Q1
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / P1
Keep the negative sign. A demand elasticity of -1.5 should be written as -1.5 so the grader can see you know demand slopes down.

Classification
- E below -1 (for example -1.5): elastic
- E between -1 and 0: inelastic
- E equal to -1: for this course, treat unit elastic as elastic, since the revenue logic is the same.

Practice example: the Quad coffee cart
The cart raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60 and daily sales fall from 500 to 400 cups.
% change in Q = -100 / 500 = -20%
% change in P = 0.60 / 3.00 = 20%
E = -20% / 20% = -1.00, so demand here is elastic (unit elastic counts as elastic).

Total revenue
Revenue before: $1,500 per day. Revenue after: $1,440 per day. Because the cart is on the elastic side, revenue moves in the opposite direction from price.

Exam tips
- On Midterm 2 either the original-value method or the midpoint method gets full credit, so use whichever is faster for you.
- A formula sheet will be stapled to the back of Midterm 2, so you do not need to memorize the formulas.
- Cross-price elasticity: take the absolute value, same as own-price, and report it to two decimals.
- If a question does not say which price is the starting price, use the lower price as the base.

Office hours for recitation questions: Fridays 1-2 pm, Econ Commons table 4.

DLEC-CTX-I1.title: Rennick Library group study room policy
DLEC-CTX-I1.text:
Rennick Library - Group Study Room Policy (Fall Term)

Group study rooms on floors 2 and 3 of Rennick Library can be reserved by current students through the library booking portal. Each room holds between four and eight people and has a wall-mounted display and a whiteboard.

Booking rules
- Reservations open seven days in advance at 8:00 am.
- Each student may hold up to two hours of bookings per day and six hours per week.
- A room is released to the waitlist if nobody from the group checks in at the front desk within 15 minutes of the start time.
- Rooms 3B and 3C are quiet rooms: whiteboard work only, no calls or video meetings.

During exam weeks
- The daily limit drops to 90 minutes so more groups get a turn.
- Overnight booking between midnight and 7:00 am is available only on floor 2.

Care of rooms
- Wipe the whiteboard and take your rubbish with you when you leave.
- Food is not allowed; covered drinks are fine.
- Report broken displays or dried-out markers at the front desk or through the portal's "Report a problem" link.

Repeated no-shows (three in one term) suspend booking privileges for two weeks. Questions: ask at the Rennick front desk or contact the circulation team through the library website.

DLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Week 6 slides - Price elasticity of demand
DLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Week 6 Lecture Slides: Price Elasticity of Demand
Prof. Adaeze Okonkwo-Hale | Harlow State University | Section 002

Slide 1 - Learning goals
- Compute own-price elasticity of demand using the course's midpoint convention
- Classify demand as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic
- Connect elasticity to what happens to total revenue when price changes

Slide 2 - Definition
Own-price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in the good's own price:
E = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price)
Because demand slopes down, the raw ratio is negative.

Slide 3 - ECON 214 convention (read this carefully)
In this course we ALWAYS use the midpoint (arc) formula unless a question explicitly says "point elasticity":
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / ((Q1 + Q2) / 2)
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / ((P1 + P2) / 2)
We report own-price elasticity as an absolute value, rounded to two decimals. So you write 1.22, not -1.22.
Many textbooks (including the optional Marchetti text) divide by the starting values instead. That gives a different number for the same data, and it gives a different number depending on whether the price goes up or down. The midpoint version gives the same answer in both directions, which is why we use it.

Slide 4 - Classification (using the absolute value |E|)
- |E| > 1: elastic
- |E| < 1: inelastic
- |E| = 1 exactly: unit elastic
Note: 1.00 after rounding counts as unit elastic on problem sets and exams.

Slide 5 - Worked example: the Quad coffee cart
The coffee cart outside Benning Hall raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60. Daily sales fall from 500 cups to 400 cups.
Step 1: % change in Q = (400 - 500) / 450 = -0.2222, i.e. -22.2%
Step 2: % change in P = (3.60 - 3.00) / 3.30 = 0.1818, i.e. 18.2%
Step 3: E = -22.2% / 18.2% = -1.22
Step 4: report |E| = 1.22, so demand is elastic over this range.
Check: with the starting-value method you would get -20% / 20% = -1.00 and call it unit elastic. Same data, different classification. This is exactly why we fix one convention.

Slide 6 - Elasticity and total revenue
Total revenue TR = P x Q.
Before: $3.00 x 500 = $1,500 per day. After: $3.60 x 400 = $1,440 per day.
Rule: when demand is elastic, a price increase lowers total revenue; when demand is inelastic, a price increase raises total revenue; at unit elasticity total revenue does not change.
The coffee cart is consistent with the rule: elastic demand, price went up, revenue fell by $60 a day.

Slide 7 - What makes demand more elastic?
- Close substitutes are available (the dining hall sells drip coffee for $2.25)
- The good is a larger share of the budget
- A longer time horizon to adjust
- A narrowly defined market ("drip coffee at this cart" versus "caffeine")

Slide 8 - Exam notes
- Midterm 2 covers Weeks 5 to 8. Elasticity questions on Midterm 2 must use the midpoint formula; answers that use starting values get at most half credit.
- Show all four steps from Slide 5.
- The elasticity formula sheet is NOT provided on Midterm 2. Memorize the formulas.

Slide 9 - Preview of Week 7
Cross-price elasticity: the sign matters there (positive means substitutes, negative means complements), so we do NOT take absolute values for cross-price elasticity.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: simpler please
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): teach me build-heap properly using his worked example: why we start at floor(n/2), what each sift-down does to the array, and why the whole thing is O(n) and not O(n log n).

NATIVELY: Build-heap works bottom-up because every index past floor(n/2) is a leaf, and a single node is already a valid heap. So we start at the last internal node and sift down toward the root.

In the example, n = 7, so we begin at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only fall a short distance. Summing each node's height gives a linear bound.
items.answer:
Build-heap goes bottom-up because the back half of the array is all leaves, and a lone leaf is already a valid heap, so there's nothing to fix there. That's why we start at floor(n/2), the last node that actually has a child.

In his example n = 7, so we start at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only fall a short distance. Add up every node's height and the total grows linearly with n.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: the handout says the coffee cart is unit elastic at -1.00 but I'm pretty sure she said elastic in lecture. which one is right, what should I write on the midterm, and why would they come out different?
items.answer:
Write **elastic**. The handout's own classification rule says that for this course, E equal to -1 is treated as elastic, since the revenue logic is the same, and the coffee cart example lands at exactly -1.00, so it's elastic.

They only look different because of the label, not the math. The number is -1.00 either way, which is unit elastic by the strict definition, but this course folds unit elastic into the elastic bucket. So on the midterm, say elastic and show the -1.00, and you're covered.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: why n/2?
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): she wrote T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) for merge sort and I have no idea how to read that

NATIVELY: That's a recurrence, a way of writing how much work an algorithm does in terms of itself. Read it as: to sort n items, merge sort splits them into two halves, sorts each half, and then merges the two sorted halves back together.

So **T(n)** is the total time for n items. The **2T(n/2)** means two subproblems, each half the size. The **Theta(n)** is the merge step, which takes time proportional to n because you walk through all the elements once. The base case, usually T(1) = constant, is implied.

If you want the intuition for why it comes out to Theta(n log n): the splitting creates log n levels, and each level does a total of about n work across all its pieces, so n times log n.
items.answer: The n/2 is the size of each half. When you split n items into two equal halves, each half has n/2 items, so the two subproblems are each of size n/2, which is why it's 2T(n/2). The 2 out front counts the two halves, and the n/2 inside T is how big each one is.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Okay so most of the ATP in the cell comes from oxidative phosphorylation in the mitochondria, and that happens across the inner membrane, which is why the inner membrane is folded up into all these cristae.
items.answer: Right, and the folding matters because it packs a lot of inner membrane into a small volume, so there's more surface area for the electron transport chain and ATP synthase to sit in. The cristae are basically where that machinery is concentrated. One thing worth adding: the ATP is made on the matrix side of the inner membrane, and the proton gradient that drives it is built up across that same membrane, so the folding and the chemistry go together.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: And that's why the firm's short-run supply curve is just its marginal cost curve, but only the part above the minimum of AVC.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Remember from Tuesday, marginal cost is what it costs to make one more unit, and the MC curve crosses average variable cost at its minimum.
PROFESSOR: And the shutdown rule: in the short run a firm keeps producing as long as price covers average variable cost, not average total cost. Fixed costs are sunk either way.
PROFESSOR: Okay, let's draw the firm's cost curves again.
items.answer: The short-run supply curve is the marginal cost curve above the minimum of average variable cost because of how a competitive firm chooses output. It sets price equal to marginal cost, so every point on MC tells you how much it supplies at that price. But below the minimum of AVC, price doesn't even cover variable cost, so the firm shuts down and supplies zero instead. That's why only the portion of MC above that minimum counts as the supply curve.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: wait he just said left child is 2i+1 but the notes say something else. what did he mean, and which formulas do I use on the quiz?
conversation: PROFESSOR: Okay, so to get from a node to its children you just do the arithmetic.
PROFESSOR: Left child of i is at 2i plus 1, right child at 2i plus 2, and the parent is i minus 1 over 2, rounded down.
items.answer: He's using the 0-indexed layout, where left is 2i+1. The notes use the 1-indexed layout, where index 0 is left empty and left is 2i, right is 2i+1, parent is floor(i/2). Both are correct for their own layout, but on the CS 261 quiz you use the **1-indexed** formulas.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Okay. So if you want the derivative of sine x from first principles, you write sine of x plus h, expand it with the angle addition formula, and the whole thing comes down to two limits: sine h over h, and cosine h minus one over h.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Before we start, quick housekeeping. The problem set deadline moved to Monday at noon because of the fire drill.
PROFESSOR: Also the Hendry Hall parking lot is closed this week, so give yourselves extra time.
items.answer:
The lecturer is sketching the first-principles proof, so here's the full derivation.

Start with the limit definition:

f'(x) = lim(h→0) [sin(x+h) − sin(x)] / h

Expand sin(x+h) with the angle addition formula:

sin(x+h) = sin x cos h + cos x sin h

Substitute and group the terms:

[sin x cos h + cos x sin h − sin x] / h = sin x · (cos h − 1)/h + cos x · (sin h)/h

So the derivative splits into the two limits the lecturer named:

f'(x) = sin x · lim(h→0)(cos h − 1)/h + cos x · lim(h→0)(sin h)/h

Those two limits are the standard ones: sin h / h → 1, and (cos h − 1)/h → 0. Plugging in:

f'(x) = sin x · 0 + cos x · 1 = **cos x**

The intuition: the sin h / h limit carries the cosine term, and the (cos h − 1)/h limit vanishes, which is why the sine's derivative comes out as cosine with no leftover sine term.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: is this on the exam?

What I can say is that anything the lecturer has emphasized, repeated, or tied to a worked example is usually fair game. If you can share the syllabus or the topics covered so far, I can help you figure out what's most likely to come up.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Now repeat it forever.
conversation: PROFESSOR (heard): Classic prisoner's dilemma. Each prisoner does better by confessing no matter what the other one does, so they both confess, even though both staying quiet would leave them better off.

NATIVELY: That's the core of it. Confessing is the **dominant strategy**: whatever the other prisoner does, you get a lighter sentence by confessing than by staying quiet. So rational self-interest drives both to confess, and they land on a worse outcome than if they'd both stayed silent. The tension is that the individually rational choice produces a collectively worse result, which is why it's a dilemma rather than just a bad decision.
items.answer: That's the **iterated prisoner's dilemma**: play the same game over and over with the same partner, and the logic shifts. When the game repeats, each player can respond to what the other did last round, so cooperation becomes sustainable. The key result is that a **tit-for-tat** strategy, cooperate first and then copy whatever your partner did, tends to do well, because it rewards cooperation and punishes defection without staying angry. Defecting once still pays in that single round, but it invites retaliation in every round after, so the long-run incentive flips toward cooperating.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: So in the trial the p-value came out at 0.03, and what that tells us is there's only a three percent chance the null hypothesis is true.
items.answer:
That's actually a common misreading. A p-value of 0.03 means that **if the null hypothesis were true**, there'd be a 3% chance of seeing data at least as extreme as what you got. It's the probability of the data given the null, not the probability of the null given the data.

So it doesn't tell you there's a 3% chance the null is true. To get that, you'd need a Bayesian posterior, which also depends on your prior. What the p-value does let you say is that the result is unlikely under the null, which is why we'd typically reject it at the 0.05 level.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: ok so what does it solve to, and show me how you get there
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): she wrote T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) for merge sort and I have no idea how to read that

NATIVELY: That's a recurrence, a way of writing how much work an algorithm does in terms of itself. Read it as: to sort n items, merge sort splits them into two halves, sorts each half, and then merges the two sorted halves back together.

So **T(n)** is the total time for n items. The **2T(n/2)** means two subproblems, each half the size. The **Theta(n)** is the merge step, which takes time proportional to n because you walk through all the elements once. The base case, usually T(1) = constant, is implied.

If you want the intuition for why it comes out to Theta(n log n): the splitting creates log n levels, and each level does a total of about n work across all its pieces, so n times log n.
USER (typed to Natively): why n/2?

NATIVELY: The n/2 is the size of each half. When you split n items into two equal halves, each half has n/2 items, so the two subproblems are each of size n/2, which is why it's 2T(n/2). The 2 out front counts the two halves, and the n/2 inside T is how big each one is.
items.answer:
To solve it, you keep expanding the recurrence until the subproblems hit the base case, then add up the work at each level.

Level 0: one problem of size n, doing Theta(n) work.
Level 1: two problems of size n/2, each doing Theta(n/2), so 2 times n/2 = Theta(n) total.
Level 2: four problems of size n/4, each doing Theta(n/4), so 4 times n/4 = Theta(n) total.

Every level costs Theta(n). The splitting stops when the pieces reach size 1, which takes log base 2 of n levels. So the total is n times log n, giving **Theta(n log n)**.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: Le Chatelier's principle: if you disturb a system at equilibrium, it shifts in the direction that partly undoes the disturbance.
items.answer: Le Chatelier's principle says a system at equilibrium pushes back against whatever you do to it. If you add more of a reactant, the reaction shifts toward the products to use it up. If you raise the pressure on a gas reaction, it shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules. If you heat it, it shifts in the endothermic direction, the one that absorbs the extra heat. The shift is only partial, so it eases the disturbance without fully cancelling it.

items.question: And the printing press is the key here, Gutenberg's from around 1450, which is why Luther's Ninety-five Theses in 1517 spread across the German lands in a matter of weeks.
items.answer: Gutenberg's movable-type press, around 1450, is what made that speed possible. Before it, texts were copied by hand or printed from carved blocks, so a single document took months to reproduce. With reusable metal type, hundreds of copies of the Ninety-five Theses could be run off in days, which is why they reached across the German lands in weeks rather than years.

items.question: And this is why industry loves catalysts, right? You add a catalyst to the contact process and it pushes the equilibrium over toward sulfur trioxide, so you end up with a higher yield.
items.answer:
That's a common mix-up, and it's worth correcting. A catalyst speeds up the rate at which the reaction reaches equilibrium, but it doesn't shift the position of equilibrium at all. It lowers the activation energy for both the forward and the reverse reaction equally, so the equilibrium constant stays the same and the yield is unchanged.

In the contact process, the catalyst is vanadium(V) oxide, and it's there to get the reaction to equilibrium fast enough to be practical. The yield is actually pushed up by other things: using excess oxygen, and running at a relatively low temperature, since the forward reaction is exothermic. The trade-off is that low temperature also slows the rate, which is exactly why you need the catalyst.

items.question: So remember, when demand is elastic and you raise the price, total revenue goes up, and that's exactly why the cart owner did it.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Okay, back to the coffee cart outside Benning Hall. Price goes from three dollars to three sixty.
PROFESSOR: Sales drop from five hundred cups a day to four hundred, and with our midpoint formula that's an elasticity of one point two two.
PROFESSOR: So demand is elastic over that range.
items.answer: The lecturer's rule is backwards here. When demand is elastic, a price increase **lowers** total revenue, not raises it. The cart's own numbers show it: $3.00 × 500 = $1,500 a day before, and $3.60 × 400 = $1,440 after, so revenue fell by $60. The rule is that elastic demand plus a price hike cuts revenue, and inelastic demand plus a price hike raises it. So the cart owner's move actually cost them money, which is the opposite of what was just said.

items.answer:

If you're already comfortable with inner joins and basic two-table syntax, the intro recap is usually skimmable. items.question: So the Peace of Westphalia, 1648, ends the Thirty Years' War, and it's usually taught as the moment the modern system of sovereign states is born.
items.answer: The Peace of Westphalia is actually a pair of treaties signed in Münster and Osnabrück, and what it did was end the Thirty Years' War and settle the overlapping religious and dynastic conflicts that had torn apart the Holy Roman Empire. The "birth of the sovereign state" reading comes from the idea that it recognized each prince's authority over religion and territory within his own lands, which later got read back as the principle of non-interference in a state's internal affairs. Historians push back on that, though, because the settlement still left the Empire's structure and the emperor's role intact, so it's less a clean founding moment than a step in a longer shift toward territorial sovereignty.

items.question: explain gradient descent using an example from my own work experience so it actually sticks
items.answer:
Gradient descent is just walking downhill in small steps. You pick a starting point, check which way the slope goes, take a small step that direction, and repeat until you stop improving.

Think of tuning something by hand: you nudge it one way, see if the result gets better, then nudge again. The step size is the learning rate. Too big and you overshoot, too small and it takes forever.

items.question: what did she mean by 'the corridor is really just a floor'?
conversation: PROFESSOR: The Fed doesn't really set 'the interest rate.' It sets a target range for the federal funds rate.
PROFESSOR: Back when reserves were scarce, it hit that target with open market operations, buying and selling securities pretty much every day.
PROFESSOR: Now we're in an ample reserves regime, so the main tool is the interest rate on reserve balances, and honestly the corridor is really just a floor.
items.answer: She means the "corridor" of rates around the target isn't a true two-sided band anymore. In an ample reserves regime, the interest rate on reserve balances acts as a floor: it sets the lowest rate banks will lend at, so the effective rate sits at or just above it rather than floating freely between a ceiling and a floor.

items.question: she wrote T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) for merge sort and I have no idea how to read that
items.answer:
That's a recurrence, a way of writing how much work an algorithm does in terms of itself. Read it as: to sort n items, merge sort splits them into two halves, sorts each half, and then merges the two sorted halves back together.

So **T(n)** is the total time for n items. The **2T(n/2)** means two subproblems, each half the size. The **Theta(n)** is the merge step, which takes time proportional to n because you walk through all the elements once. The base case, usually T(1) = constant, is implied.

If you want the intuition for why it comes out to Theta(n log n): the splitting creates log n levels, and each level does a total of about n work across all its pieces, so n times log n.
